name: Modified GRF (1-29)

lead: Modified GRF (1-29), also called Mod GRF or CJC-1295 without DAC, is a lab-made fragment of GHRH tweaked to resist breakdown. Users pair it with a growth hormone-releasing peptide to get short pulses of growth hormone, aiming for better sleep and recovery, more muscle and a leaner look.

It stimulates GHRH receptors on pituitary cells, releasing growth hormone in a brief pulse. Hormone studies describe the two peptide types working together to release more growth hormone than either alone. No clinical trial cited has tested it for appearance, and user reports are anecdotal and mixed.

paras: Forum users describe it as the GHRH half of a pairing with GHRP-2, GHRP-6 or ipamorelin. Because it is short-acting, it is used to mimic natural pulses of growth hormone, with users reporting sleep, recovery and body-composition changes over weeks.

It is unapproved and listed as prohibited in sport. A Danish forensic analysis of seized powders found products sold as modified GRF (1-29) contained analogues with an extra glycine added, so what is sold online can differ from the label.

angle.text: Mod GRF (CJC-1295 without DAC) is paired with a GH-releasing peptide to give short growth hormone pulses, with users citing better sleep, recovery and a leaner, more muscular look. The pairing's synergy is described in hormone studies; human trials for appearance have not been run.

lead: Modified GRF (1-29), also called Mod GRF, tetrasubstituted GRF (1-29) and CJC-1295 without DAC, is a synthetic 29-amino-acid analogue of the active fragment of growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH). Four amino acid substitutions are described as making it more resistant to enzymatic breakdown than the natural sequence.[1][2] It is not approved as a medicine.

People who use it do so to raise their own growth hormone release, with the aim of building muscle, losing body fat, sleeping and recovering better and, in some posts on looksmax.org, gaining height.[3][4] The chain they describe runs from pituitary stimulation to larger growth hormone pulses and higher IGF-1, and from there to a leaner, more muscular physique. In bodybuilding and peptide forums it is typically described as the GHRH half of a pairing with a growth hormone-releasing peptide (GHRP) such as GHRP-2, GHRP-6 or ipamorelin, with users reporting that the two together release more growth hormone than either alone.[5][4][6][7][8][9]

No published clinical trial has tested Modified GRF (1-29) itself for muscle, fat loss or appearance. Human studies exist for related molecules, notably the long-acting DAC version CJC-1295 and the parent peptide GRF (1-29), and these are described below under Clinical studies.[2][10] A Danish forensic study of seized doping powders found that products sold as modified GRF (1-29) and other secretagogues contained analogues with an extra glycine added, showing that material sold online can differ from the labelled compound.[11]
infobox: Mod GRF 1-29, tetrasubstituted GRF(1-29), CJC-1295 no DAC[1][10]
At least 30 minutes (native GRF 1-29: under 10 minutes)[2]
Not approved as a medicine; CJC-1295 is on WADA's prohibited list per Wikipedia's categorisation[10]

paras: Modified GRF (1-29) corresponds to the first 29 residues of the 44-residue human GHRH, the part responsible for receptor binding, with substitutions at positions 2, 8, 15 and 27.[1][2] Wikipedia lists them as D-alanine for alanine at position 2, glutamine for asparagine at 8, alanine for glycine at 15 and leucine for methionine at 27.[2] An AI-generated encyclopedia entry states that these changes protect it from cleavage by dipeptidyl peptidase-IV and that it was developed in the early 2000s by ConjuChem Biotechnologies; the entry is not a primary source.[1]

It is distinguished from CJC-1295 with DAC (drug affinity complex), which carries an additional maleimidopropionyl-lysine group at position 30 that binds albumin and prolongs its action; Wikipedia gives an estimated half-life of about 6 to 8 days for the DAC form.[10] The parent GRF (1-29), also called sermorelin, has a half-life of under 10 minutes, possibly as short as 5, while the modified analogue's half-life is at least 30 minutes according to Wikipedia.[2] Wikipedia's CJC-1295 article also notes that the names CJC-1295 and Modified GRF (1-29) are sometimes confused in scientific papers, which is one source of mixed terminology in forums.[10] A 1992 patent family describes amino-terminal-modified GRF analogues with superior activity and potency compared to native GRF, illustrating the longer research history of this class.[12]

Modified GRF (1-29) acts by binding the growth hormone-releasing hormone receptor on anterior pituitary cells, increasing production and release of growth hormone.[2] Wikipedia traces the background to 1983 and 1984 studies showing that the first 29 amino acids of GHRH were as potent as the full molecule, and notes that the fragment cleared quickly because plasma enzymes degraded it to an inactive product, prompting analogues with substitutions that resist enzymes.[2] An early change replacing L-alanine at position 2 with D-alanine blocked cleavage by dipeptidyl peptidase-4; a 1994 study in men reported that D-Ala2 substitution increased half-life and decreased metabolic clearance.[2]

Proponents describe the no-DAC peptide as producing a short pulse of growth hormone that mimics the body's natural pulsatile secretion, in contrast to the sustained elevation of the DAC form.[1] An AI-generated encyclopedia entry reports in vitro work in rat pituitary cells and rodent studies of growth hormone and IGF-1 elevation, which were not verified against primary papers.[1]

GHRH was isolated in 1982 by a team led by Roger Guillemin from a pancreatic tumour in a patient with acromegaly, according to Grokipedia, after which the 1-29 fragment was found to be as potent as the full peptide.[1][2] In 2005, Jetté and colleagues described the tetrasubstituted version in a study of GRF (1-29) analogues and identified CJC-1295 as a long-lasting analogue in rats; Wikipedia reports this as the first specific description of the tetrasubstituted form in the literature.[2][10]

In March 2006 Teichman and colleagues published a human study of CJC-1295 in healthy adults reporting that a single dose raised growth hormone two- to ten-fold for six days or longer and IGF-1 0.5- to 3-fold for 9 to 11 days; multiple doses kept IGF-1 raised for up to 28 days, according to Wikipedia. Ionescu and Frohman reported later that year that pulsatile growth hormone secretion persisted during continuous stimulation.[10] Phase II trials of CJC-1295 for lipodystrophy and growth hormone deficiency were stopped after one participant died; the attending physician believed the death was due to asymptomatic coronary artery disease and unrelated to the drug, and research was ended as a precaution.[10]

T Nation threads discuss GHRH analogues from 2009 onward, and a 2020 thread on CJC-1295 quotes a description of the DAC version as developed by ConjuChem Biotechnologies with improved half-life.[4][13]

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities
paras: On T Nation, Modified GRF (1-29) is discussed from around 2009 onward as the preferred GHRH analogue among those then available, usually paired with GHRP-2 or GHRP-6. Users describe taking GHRP-plus-GRF combinations at different times of day, sometimes alongside testosterone, trenbolone or other peptides in logged cycles.[4][7][5][6][9][11][14]

Reports of results are mixed in tone. One user who finished a roughly 40-day run of GHRP-2 and Modified GRF said they could not tell whether it worked and described feeling unwell after doses, while another reports improved sleep quality after several months.[5][7]

On looksmax.org, threads on CJC-1295 without DAC with ipamorelin discuss it in connection with height. One poster described a flushed feeling after doses, and when asked why they were using it, said they were trying to get height gains; another user answered that this was a cope.[3] Other threads titled as protocols or usage guides appear in the forum's peptide section.[15][16] The wider appeal in appearance forums is the muscle, leanness and recovery chain: more growth hormone and IGF-1 is expected to support training, fat loss and sleep, which in turn shape physique.[4][7]

The forensic study of seized material found that the powders analysed carried an extra glycine at the N-terminus, so that analytical methods for secretagogues needed updating, which indicates variability between labelled and actual content.[11] Wikipedia notes that a 2010 study identified CJC-1295 in an unknown pharmaceutical preparation and that peptide compounds were confiscated in Denmark between 2007 and 2013.[10]

The US Food and Drug Administration maintains a list of peptide bulk drug substances that may present significant safety risks for compounding. As of its 2026 update, FDA lists GHRP-2, GHRP-6 and ipamorelin acetate in Category 2 (dated September 29, 2023), citing possible immunogenicity from aggregation and impurities, and says CJC-1295 was nominated and then withdrawn, noting serious adverse events including increased heart rate and systemic vasodilation and limited clinical data. Modified GRF (1-29) is not an FDA-approved drug.[1] An AI-generated encyclopedia entry says it is prohibited in sport by WADA, and Wikipedia categorises CJC-1295 among WADA prohibited substances.[1][10]

No studies found for Modified GRF (1-29) itself for appearance, muscle or fat loss. Related human work concerns the parent and long-acting analogues. Wikipedia's references include a 1984 study of responses to GRF analogues in normal subjects and in growth-hormone-deficient children and young adults and a 1994 study of D-Ala2 substitution in normal men.[2] The 2006 Teichman study of the DAC form CJC-1295 in healthy adults measured growth hormone and IGF-1 responses rather than body composition or appearance.[10]

Related published material on the modified compound concerns chemistry and forensic detection rather than clinical effects, such as the 2019 report of glycine-modified secretagogue analogues, including modified GRF (1-29), in seized material.[11]

Sermorelin (GRF 1-29), CJC-1295 with DAC, tesamorelin and the growth hormone-releasing peptides GHRP-2, GHRP-6, hexarelin and ipamorelin form the cluster of GH-axis compounds discussed alongside Modified GRF (1-29).[2][10] Forum users pair GHRH analogues with GHRPs on the reasoning that the two act on different pathways and together release more growth hormone than either alone.[5][7][8]

lore.intro: On T Nation, Mod GRF 1-29 is mentioned in peptide stacks, usually as the GHRH half of a GHRP/GHRH pairing; on looksmax.org it appears in height-related peptide threads.[5][4][7][3]
